body:
I agree that support for input masking would really help a lot of specific kinds of input, especially long fields of nondescript numbers like credit card or serial numbers.

Our product serial numbers are in the form XXXX-XXXXX, which is much easier to read at a glance than one great big uninterrupted string. This is even more obvious when it's a 25-digit product key in groups of five, for instance.

Without support for input masking, it's very tempting to implement these fields as multiple separate fields with a bunch of Javascript to support pasting, automatically advancing through the fields as you type or backspace, etc., all of which makes the end result harder to support accessibly, and very different from website to website, depending on how conscientious the developer was.

Implemented properly, this should be able to degrade gracefully on older browsers, but provide a natural UX improvement for modern UAs.

I think we should mimic existing implementations. I am a JS/TS only developer, but my dad uses Delphi. When he needs masking, it is a property of the input. .NET also has some implementation.

<details>

<summary>The mask definition from .NET: (I think it is also the same that Excel uses)</summary>

| Masking element      | Description                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 0                    | Digit, required. This element will accept any single digit between 0 and 9.                                                                                                                   |
| 9                    | Digit or space, optional.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| #                    | Digit or space, optional. If this position is blank in the mask, it will be rendered as a space in the Text property. Plus (+) and minus (-) signs are allowed.                               |
| L                    | Letter, required. Restricts input to the ASCII letters a-z and A-Z. This mask element is equivalent to [a-zA-Z] in regular expressions.                                                       |
| ?                    | Letter, optional. Restricts input to the ASCII letters a-z and A-Z. This mask element is equivalent to [a-zA-Z]? in regular expressions.                                                      |
| &                    | Character, required. If the AsciiOnly property is set to true, this element behaves like the "L" element.                                                                                     |
| C                    | Character, optional. Any non-control character. If the AsciiOnly property is set to true, this element behaves like the "?" element.                                                          |
| A                    | Alphanumeric, required. If the AsciiOnly property is set to true, the only characters it will accept are the ASCII letters a-z and A-Z. This mask element behaves like the "a" element.       |
| a                    | Alphanumeric, optional. If the AsciiOnly property is set to true, the only characters it will accept are the ASCII letters a-z and A-Z. This mask element behaves like the "A" element.       |
| .                    | Decimal placeholder. The actual display character used will be the decimal symbol appropriate to the format provider, as determined by the control's FormatProvider property.                 |
| ,                    | Thousands placeholder. The actual display character used will be the thousands placeholder appropriate to the format provider, as determined by the control's FormatProvider property.        |
| :                    | Time separator. The actual display character used will be the time symbol appropriate to the format provider, as determined by the control's FormatProvider property.                         |
| /                    | Date separator. The actual display character used will be the date symbol appropriate to the format provider, as determined by the control's FormatProvider property.                         |
| $                    | Currency symbol. The actual character displayed will be the currency symbol appropriate to the format provider, as determined by the control's FormatProvider property.                       |
| <                    | Shift down. Converts all characters that follow to lowercase.                                                                                                                                 |
| >                    | Shift up. Converts all characters that follow to uppercase.                                                                                                                                   |
| \|                   | Disable a previous shift up or shift down.                                                                                                                                                    |
| \                    | Escape. Escapes a mask character, turning it into a literal. "\" is the escape sequence for a backslash.                                                                                      |
| All other characters | Literals. All non-mask elements will appear as themselves within MaskedTextBox. Literals always occupy a static position in the mask at run time, and cannot be moved or deleted by the user. |

</details>

The Intl could still be used in the way that it could have 2 functions: 
* `Intl.generateMask(maskName: PreDefinedMaskNames, options?: Intl.MaskOptions): string`, This would generate the masked string based on the locale
* `Intl.validateMask(mask: string, inputToValidate: string): boolean` validate input against mask

The stated use cases and the linked JS libraries seem to be about the input consisting only of ASCII digits. The .NET syntax from the previous comment gives special status to some more ASCII characters.

It would be interesting to know if the .NET implementation behaves usefully with scripts that don't have one-to-one mapping between key strokes and extended grapheme clusters. It would also be interesting to know to what extent use cases are constrained to 1) ASCII digits, 2) ASCII, or 3) characters that come with a single key stroke (potentially with a modifier key like shift pressed) on a locale-relevant keyboard layout.

It would probably make sense to try to solve this first for ASCII digits with ASCII punctuation (such as plus sign at the start of a phone number), but with a plan for how the solution does not prevent extension to more kinds of characters subsequently.

The original "Why" was about "Masking input to look like a phone, credit card, postal code". Person or street names are something very different. It's generally an antipattern to limit them for allowed characters, so it's problematic to design Web Platform surface for the purpose of constraining person or street names (even if surfacing the constraints of a legacy back end might in some case be less bad than not surfacing the constraints in the front end and failing later).

Having masks support ASCII digits and ASCII punctuation avoids the problem of ASCII-minded developers using masks for person or street names. It would be problematic to add support ASCII letters without adding even more at the same time, though. (There's a handful of postal code domains in the world, 11 out of 160 per Wikipedia, that use alphanumeric postal codes, so not doing letters at first would prevent the use of masks for e.g. UK postal codes.)

Another related (but meaningfully different) direction: [“segmented input”](https://jimmywarting.github.io/segmented-input/).

the are "kind of" the same but still different in some ways.

Instead of a single text field with a formatting mask, segmented input treats one logical value as multiple editable sub-fields (segments) with explicit per-segment constraints. Visually it can still look like one control, but behaviorally it’s closer to how <input type=date> (and time) expose multiple editable parts inside one widget.

Why this differs from a string mask:
- Each segment has its own length/charset constraints (e.g. digits only, fixed width, range constraints).
- Users can navigate between segments with Tab / Shift+Tab / Arrow keys, and selection/caret behavior is segment-aware (no “caret stuck inside punctuation” problems).
- Deletion/backspace semantics become simpler and more predictable because separators aren’t “characters” in the same editable stream.
- Better AT / IME / virtual keyboard story is possible because the UA can expose structure (e.g. “area code”, “prefix”, “line number”) instead of a single opaque string.
- Autocomplete could also be segment-aware (fill one segment, or all), and UAs can render separators/styling without it being part of the value.

This can cover many of the common “mask” use-cases (phone, credit card, postal codes, national IDs), but with more explicit structure and navigation.

I built a library to which is a general-purpose-solution-to-fit-them-all 
https://github.com/jimmywarting/segmented-input/

i know that it's kind of like a masked input. but each "segment" has it's own validation and control / logic / validation. hence why i called it "segmented input" and not "yet another masked input" library. it closely behave more like a `<input type="date">` input rather than any of the masked inputs
